chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The one who eats and is grateful, for him is a reward like the reward of the fasting one who counts his reward [with God]; and the one who is healthy and is grateful, for him is a reward like the reward of the afflicted one who is patient; and the one who is given [bounties] and is grateful, for him is a reward like the reward of the deprived one who is content.'
ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for being grateful in health, wealth, and eating?
ai.summary: Recorded in Al-Kafi, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the dynamic nature of spiritual merit, where gratitude acts as a multiplier that elevates the status of the comfortable to match the reward of the ascetic. It highlights the Shia emphasis on 'muhasabah' (self-accounting) and 'qana'ah' (contentment), suggesting that conscious appreciation transforms mundane acts like eating into worship comparable to fasting. This teaching underscores that spiritual rank is determined not merely by external conditions but by the internal state of thankfulness and awareness of God's blessings.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Al Nowfaly, from Al Sakuny, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘Rasool-Allah<sup>saww</sup> said: ‘The feeder of the food, the grateful, for him would be the Recompense like the Recompense of the Fasting one bringing himself to account; and the one of good health, the grateful, for him would be from the Recompense like the Recompense of the afflicted one (with illness), the patient; and the Given one, the grateful, for him would be from the Recompense, like the Recompense of the deprived one, the contented’.
en.sarwar: 1. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from al-Nawfali from al-Sakuni from abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) who has said the following: “

The Messenger of Allah has said, ‘A person feeding (himself) with gratitude (before Allah) has a reward equal to the reward of a fasting person who brings himself to strict account. A person in good health who is grateful receives a reward equal to the reward of a person who suffers from an illness but exercises patience. A person who gives charity with gratitude receives a reward equal to the reward of a deprived person who is content.’”
